pr_title: Remove local fork of archive/tar package
pr_body:
**- What I did**
Removed the local fork of `archive/tar` while retaining all existing mitigations of CVE-2019-14271. Fixes #42402

**- How I did it**
I hid the value containing the file's UID and GID from the `tar.FileInfoHeader` function [so that it would elide calling `user.LookupId`](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.17.6:src/archive/tar/stat_unix.go;l=28-31), analogous to the proposal in golang/go#50102.

**- How to verify it**
1. Comment out [the other mitigation](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/559ff0ac661c1ca27bb17765629f6166d90ff499/pkg/chrootarchive/archive.go#L15-L20) and [the mitigation introduced in this PR](https://github.com/corhere/moby/blob/0ef67c6a9bdc7420210318fcef4fe0af3fc0cac6/pkg/archive/archive.go#L413-L421) and `make dynbinary`
2. Build a container image which exploits CVE-2019-14271 (an exploit payload which prints a message to stderr and exits nonzero makes it easy to spot in `dockerd`'s debug logs) and create a container from that image
3. `docker cp` from the container and observe that the exploit code has been executed
4. Uncomment the mitigation from this PR (leaving the other mitigation commented out), rebuild dockerd, and try to exploit the vulnerability again. Observe that the exploit payload does not execute.

**- Description for the changelog**
Remove local fork of `archive/tar` package

**- A picture of a cute animal (not mandatory but encouraged)**
pr_comments: I am also experimenting with having a separate binary for the chrootarchive reexecs as I described in https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/42402#issuecomment-1018068519 which has both compile-time and runtime assertions to make really, really sure that it can only be built as a static binary without cgo. I have opened a draft PR for your consideration: #43186

> In view of this, perhaps it might make sense to close [golang/go#50102](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50102) since we can achieve a similar thing without too much effort.

I think the proposal should be left open. This PR implements the suggestion from https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50102#issuecomment-995070401 and reimplements the loading of (some of) the other filesystem info in userspace, so to speak. The proposed `tar.FileInfoNames` interface would reduce the amount of moby code that needs to be maintained to support new platforms, and would be beneficial to others in a similar situation who also require having atime and ctime set in their tar file headers.

The problems with this is that it:
- Makes assumptions about the stdlib `FileInfoHeader` implementation. That the current implementation has custom code for `*tar.Header` and `statUnix` implementation in stdlib returns early before it reaches the code that can invoke the libraries that do the loading of usernames. Potentially this can change without notice in stdlib.
- We need to make sure that the new `NoLookups` function is used always. If one place forgets to call it (eg. after some code change) it breaks the security for the rest. This is also true for the proposal in https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50102

If we are ok with these risks then the implementation SGTM

> The problems with this is that it:
> 
> * Makes assumptions about the stdlib `FileInfoHeader` implementation. That the current implementation has custom code for `*tar.Header` and `statUnix` implementation in stdlib returns early before it reaches the code that can invoke the libraries that do the loading of usernames. Potentially this can change without notice in stdlib.

The only assumption being made is that the stdlib `tar.FileInfoHeader` implementation loads the file's username and group name iff the file's UID and GID are known to it. The `fs.FileInfo` interface cannot be widened without breaking the Go 1 Compatibility Promise so it seems highly unlikely for the mechanism used to get the UID and GID from the `FileInfo` value to change without notice. That being said, I can guard against such an occurrence by adding a unit test which asserts that `tar.FileInfoHeader(nosysFileInfo{fi}, "")` returns a `tar.Header` with zero-valued `Uname` and `Gname` fields when `fi` is a value returned from `os.Stat`.

> * We need to make sure that the new `NoLookups` function is used always. If one place forgets to call it (eg. after some code change) it breaks the security for the rest. This is also true for the proposal in [archive/tar: add FileInfoNames interface golang/go#50102](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50102)

We need to make sure that the new function is always used in code executed inside a chroot. Or to be more precise, we need to make sure that `dlopen()` is never executed while the process is chrooted. Loading shared objects from the host's system library paths does not break security when the process's filesystem root is the host's filesystem root. And conversely, `archive/tar` is not the only package which potentially leads to `dlopen()` via glibc. Even with the existing solution of patching `archive/tar`, [security could be broken by a call to e.g. `user.Current()` or `net.Dial()` while chrooted.](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/42402#issuecomment-1015870306) Although, as I mentioned in the PR description, [there is another layer of mitigation](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/559ff0ac661c1ca27bb17765629f6166d90ff499/pkg/chrootarchive/archive.go#L15-L20) which prevents such oversights from actually breaking security.

Looks like gosec linting is complaining. We had quite some "false positives" on that linter, but we should check. We updated the linter to a new version Yesterday; if `G305`  is not useful for us, we can either disable it globally or if "useful", but not for all cases, add some `//nolint: gosec` comments, e.g.

@corhere thanks again! We discussed this PR in Yesterday's maintainers meeting with @tonistiigi @samuelkarp @cpuguy83 @tianon and @crazy-max and from that discussion, I think we're good to move forward with this change.

Could you rebase the PR (and have a look at the linter failures? https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/43185#issuecomment-1036035571)

> I can guard against such an occurrence by adding a unit test which asserts that `tar.FileInfoHeader(nosysFileInfo{fi}, "")` returns a `tar.Header` with zero-valued `Uname` and `Gname` fields when `fi` is a value returned from `os.Stat`.

It probably doesn't hurt to have a test (just to be sure); that said (as mentioned) there may be other areas that could potentially do a `dlopen()` vis `glib`; I recall we had discussions about that at the time, and there was no "real" solution other than the separate binary, which we still could consider as a follow-up.

> [there is another layer of mitigation](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/559ff0ac661c1ca27bb17765629f6166d90ff499/pkg/chrootarchive/archive.go#L15-L20) which prevents such oversights from actually breaking security.

I was actually trying to recall why we added back the vendored `pkg/archive` (after we added the other mitigation); I found https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/35739#issuecomment-379405517 on that topic, and some internal tickets, which may have been related to Docker Enterprise versions being on different go versions (not supporting the `osusergo` build tag) and/or FIPS-compliant builds of Docker Enterprise, but my memory is failing me.

Let me know if you need help!

I hope I didn't miss anything (if I did, can you add details, @tonistiigi ?)

> Could you rebase the PR (and have a look at the linter failures? [#43185 (comment)](https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/43185#issuecomment-1036035571))

On it. Taking a peek under the hood at the gosec linter, [it indiscriminately flags any `path.Join` call with an argument derived from a `tar.Header`](https://github.com/securego/gosec/blob/7d539ed49444b2c6fd83329677ba6a9b13ecb688/rules/archive.go#L20) without checking if it is followed by a mitigation for path-traversal so lots of potential for false positives. I'll review the code to verify that all the usages are safe and [annotate them with `//#nosec` suppressions](https://github.com/securego/gosec#annotating-code) as [they are more auditable than `//nolint` suppressions](https://github.com/securego/gosec#tracking-suppressions).

> It probably doesn't hurt to have a test (just to be sure)

[Done.](https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/43185/files#diff-144ed9ddaa96c27e61b10908199e330dcd263680e7a00cebc98370f370221305R1405-R1413)

> I was actually trying to recall why we added back the vendored `pkg/archive` (after we added the other mitigation); I found [#35739 (comment)](https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/35739#issuecomment-379405517) on that topic, and some internal tickets, which may have been related to Docker Enterprise versions being on different go versions (not supporting the `osusergo` build tag) and/or FIPS-compliant builds of Docker Enterprise, but my memory is failing me.

[Thankfully it was documented at the time!](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/61138fb5fc0f5fc1799cabfa86d28fb88a0f472c/vendor/archive/tar/README.md) Tl;dr it was a workaround required specifically for static builds on Go 1.10 with `CGO_ENABLED=1` which was made obsolete by Go 1.11 with the `osusergo` build tag. (Although in hindsight, `nosysFileInfo` might have been just as effective a workaround back then.) I'll follow up internally with the rest of the Mirantis Container Runtime team to verify that this change won't give us any trouble with FIPS-compliant builds, but otherwise it appears that the reasons for adding the back the vendored `archive/tar` have long reached their end of life.

> [Thankfully it was documented at the time!](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/61138fb5fc0f5fc1799cabfa86d28fb88a0f472c/vendor/archive/tar/README.md)

🤦 ah, good find! I didn't look there!

> Although in hindsight, nosysFileInfo might have been just as effective a workaround back then

If my memory serves me well, the `osusergo` option was added before the archive/tar issues existed (as it already cases grievance when using `os/user`); only before, it would happen when it was used explicitly, and now it became an issue when used implicitly (through archive/tar)
I'll go ahead and bring this one in. I assume @tonistiigi is good with this (otherwise let me know)

issue_context.title: Remove local fork of Golang's archive/tar
issue_context.body:
commit aa6a9891b09cce3d9004121294301a30d45d998d (19.03 branch) and https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/40672 (master / 20.10) re-introduced a local copy of go's archive/tar package, with a patch applied [patches/0001-archive-tar-do-not-populate-user-group-names.patch](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/841c1f338872ca37d9fe8c699336823222dba5da/patches/0001-archive-tar-do-not-populate-user-group-names.patch).

This patch was applied for the [19.03.8 release](https://github.com/docker/docker-ce/releases/tag/v19.03.8) to improve mitigation for [CVE-2019-14271](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-14271) for some nscd configuration.

We should try to get rid of this fork again.

The discussion on https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/40672#discussion_r391306456 mentioned we should open a ticket / pull request in upstream Go to make this functionality "optional", but I think @tonistiigi also had alternatives in mind to address it.
comments:
I'm definitely all for it, especially since in Go 1.17+ we're going to have a _much_ harder time maintaining this the way we currently do (and I think it already probably causes grief for packagers who don't get to use our `vendor/` as-is).

@cpuguy83 suggested that if we still need the patch we could instead maintain a proper forked package, which would be at least possible to deal with in a Go modules world, but IMO something that doesn't require forking the standard library would be awesome if there are ideas around that :sweat_smile:

> @cpuguy83 suggested that if we still need the patch we could instead maintain a proper forked package, which would be at least possible to deal with in a Go modules world...

Are we only concerned with Docker's usage of `archive/tar`, or perhaps there are some dependencies that are affected also?

> we could instead maintain a proper forked package, which would be at least possible to deal with in a Go modules world...

I would be ok with doing this for the short term (change the import paths to a package in moby (or could be a separate repo). What I wasn't sure about for this though would be if we're _able_ to replace it everywhere where we want it to be replaced; if `archive/tar` is used indirectly in Go stdlib, is there a risk of reintroducing the issue we're trying to fix?

I haven't looked deeply into that scenario, but possibly others know.

The "proper" fix of course is to propose a patch upstream to add a build-tag to disable the bits we're removing (`nouserlookup` or whatever), but likely go 1.19 would be the first chance to get that in

The alternative approach is to add something like `archivetarnonames` (to disable name lookups), but since these lookups are only done by a single function that is not used internally, it seems better to add another.

For the lack of better things to do on a Friday night, wrote a proposal: https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50102. Most probably it has errors, omissions and other issues -- please review and suggest improvements.
Thanks @kolyshkin! I added a few comments, hopefully will be somewhat helpful :)

I took a look at the situation for myself and have some possible ideas for how to get rid of the fork without regressing on the vulnerability or waiting for changes to be accepted into the upstream standard library.

The root cause of the vulnerability, AIUI, is that the cgo/POSIX implementation of `os/user` calls libc functions which, in glibc, are implemented by dynamically loading an NSS module (`libnss_*.so.2`) into the process. An attacker could trick the process into loading a malicious attacker-controlled library by setting `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` in the process's environment or dropping the malicious library into one of the default library search paths. This is not normally a security vulnerability as an attacker would need to already have enough privilege on the host that there would be no need to exploit the process: if they already have write access to one of the host's default library paths or the ability to control the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable, they would already have enough access to e.g. replace `libc.so.6`, set `LD_PRELOAD` on the process to inject their malicious code directly, or use their (most likely) root privileges to simply replace the `dockerd` binary outright.

Ironically, the hardening of moby's archiver using a chroot is what makes the dynamic loading of NSS modules into an exploitable attack vector. The attacker has full control of the entire chroot filesystem — it's a container's filesystem! If the first call to one of the `os/user` functions which triggers the loading of the NSS modules happens after pivoting into the chroot, the modules are resolved and loaded _from the attacker-controlled container filesystem._ There was an attempt to mitigate the vulnerability with #39612 which ensures that the NSS modules are loaded into the process before pivoting into the chroot. But seeing as the forking of `archive/tar` was re-added after, I can only assume that loading the host's NSS modules then pivoting into what is effectively a completely different OS userland could still break things. So the only complete fix would be to avoid calling any code which calls into the libc functions that trigger glibc to load NSS modules into the process. Building the binary with `CGO_ENABLED=0` or the `osusergo` build flag is sufficient to ensure that none of the `os/user` functions call into libc, but that has some downsides which @kolyshkin has already elaborated upon in his proposal on golang/go. Without those build configuration changes, the issues can be avoided "merely" by ensuring that the `os/user` functions are never called by the chroot'ed process. This is easier said than done.

The function `archive/tar.FileInfoHeader` calls the problematic `os/user` functions via the unexported function `tar.statUnix`, indirectly (more on that in a moment). `FileInfoHeader` is the only function which calls `statUnix`. The `FileInfoHeader` function is used by moby when creating (not extracting) archives within the chroot. And it's a leaf function: no code in Go's standard library (1.16 and 1.17) calls that function outside of tests. `FileInfoHeader` returns a `tar.Header` struct, which has no unexported members, therefore a `tar.Header` value could be fully constructed from normal application/library code. _The `FileInfoHeader` function is not strictly required._ Therefore, for application code fully under our control, an alternative implementation which doesn't call `os/user` functions can be subbed in without any trickery, patches or hacks. This could take the form of forking and patching a copy of the standard library's implementation of `tar.FileInfoHeader` (e.g. `github.com/docker/docker/internal/tarhdr`) [or writing a totally new implementation that does exactly what moby needs it to do.](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/79651b7a979b40e26af353ad283ca7ea5d67a855/pkg/archive/archive.go#L406-L425) This would Just Work... so long as there isn't any third-party code which indirectly calls `tar.FileInfoHeader` unexpectedly. Since the chroot-archive process is limited enough in scope(?) that can be audited manually, but it would be nice to have defense-in-depth. That's where patching `archive/tar` directly would be helpful. If only there was a way to do it in a Go Modules-compatible way.

The implementations of `tar.FileInfoHeader` in Go 1.16 and 1.17 just so happen to be written in such a way that the call to `tar.statUnix` can be monkeypatched with an alternative implementation at runtime. `statUnix` is called [indirectly through a function variable](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.17.6:src/archive/tar/common.go;l=701-703;bpv=1;bpt=1) which is [assigned at runtime](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.17.6:src/archive/tar/stat_unix.go;l=19-21). It's not exported, but there is an (unsafe) way to assign to it from a different package, anyway.
```go
import (
	"archive/tar"
	"io/fs"

	_ "unsafe" // required for go:linkname
)

//go:linkname sysStat archive/tar.sysStat
var sysStat func(fi fs.FileInfo, h *tar.Header) error
```
With this one ~weird trick~ little hack, moby code can assign `sysStat = nil` or `sysStat = myStatUnix` to ensure that any code calling into `tar.FileInfoHeader` anywhere in the process would not invoke the problematic libc functions! It could break between Go versions, but multiple versions of Go could be supported in the same codebase by utilizing build constraints. It is not ideal, but I think it would be a much more maintainable situation than the status quo while Go's standard library catches up.

What do you think? I would be happy to share my proof-of-concept, or open a PR which implements what I have proposed.

The big caveat for my ideas above is how brittle the defenses are: any call to an `os/user` function after the process has pivoted into the chroot could reintroduce the vulnerability. Extreme vigilance and static analysis would be required. Ideally we could robustly harden the chroot-archiver such that glibc `dlopen()`ing one of its modules while the process is chrooted cannot lead to execution of malicious code. I have some ideas on how to do just that.

[The dynamic linker](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ld.so.8.html) and [its runtime counterpart `dlopen()`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/dlopen.3.html) searches for the shared object to load by checking:
1. the directories specified in the `DT_RPATH` or `DT_RUNPATH` ELF tags embedded into the binary,
2. the directories specified in the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable,
3. for an entry in the file `/etc/ld.so.cache` specifying the path to the object,
4. in the default paths `/lib{64}` and `/usr/lib{64}`.

I believe that removing the attacker's ability to control the contents of the root directory of the chroot filesystem is sufficient to prevent them from tricking the dynamic linker into loading shared objects from within the chroot. Mounting the container's root filesystem such that it is a subdirectory of the chroot stops the attacker from controlling the contents of the trusted `/etc`, `/usr` and `/lib` trees.

The values of `DT_RPATH`, `DT_RUNPATH` and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` are not attacker-controlled in our threat model. The `DT_*` ELF tags are set when the binary is built, therefore are controlled by the packagers/distributors of moby. The value of `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` is controlled by the system administrator. We can guard against exploits via these configurations, even by a malicious administrator, by randomizing the directory name for the container filesystem's mountpoint to make it unpredictable.

-----

For more defense-in-depth, the container filesystem can be (bind-)mounted `noexec`. The Linux kernel blocks attempts to `mmap(PROT_EXEC)` memory pages from files on noexec filesystems, so even if an attacker found another way to trick the dynamic linker into loading a shared object from the container filesystem, attempts to map executable sections of the file into the process's memory space would fail. This is not yet sufficient to completely block all exploits, however, as relocations can be abused to build and execute a Return-Oriented Programming chain before the linker attempts to map any executable pages ([sourceware bugzilla](https://sourceware.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=21718), [ChromeOS issue](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1182687)). There is ongoing work on both the kernel and userland sides to plug this hole upstream ([glibc patch](https://sourceware.org/pipermail/libc-alpha/2021-July/129282.html), [kernel support](https://lwn.net/Articles/832959/)) and security-hardened systems such as ChromeOS are already incorporating patches into their distributions. Once the upstream work is complete and is incorporated into shipping systems, we would get the more robust hardening with no further changes to moby code.

-----

By mounting the container filesystem as a randomly-named subdirectory of the chroot with the `noexec` option, we can ensure that bugs in moby code which trigger dynamic linking while chrooted cannot be exploited to escape the sandbox via code execution. It would at worst result in a non-exploitable crash of the chroot-archive process. Therefore (monkey)patching the Go standard library would not be necessary. Our own custom implementation of `TarInfoHeader` would still be required, but it will no longer be the vulnerability linchpin.

Bind mounting into a safe location could work... e.g. `/tmp/tarJob-<rand>/rootfs`

Originally issue I think was that we did chroot to the rootfs as a subdir but this was within the main graphdriver dir tree and allowed the container process to use symlinks to gain access to the host.

Another layer could be putting randomized junk values into all the lookup vars. I'm not sure what glibc would do here if the value doesn't exist, though.

The more I think about it, the more uneasy I get about `chroot`ing into a hostile rootfs inside a dynamically-linked process after it has started executing. It's quite the fair assumption that the library search paths which were trusted to locate the shared libraries when the executable image was first linked and loaded will continue to be trustworthy for the duration of the process's lifetime. Any version of any shared library could `dlopen` another library as a side effect of practically anything, as an implementation detail, and it would be completely justified to do so. Any mitigations to harden docker-tar against a dynamically-linked library loading code from inside the chroot could be rendered useless without warning by a glibc upgrade, or linking against musl, or bionic. And the mitigations themselves necessarily have to be complex and clever, which are not desirable properties of security-sensitive code.

I'm really warming up to the idea of building `docker-tar` as a binary with cgo always disabled as it takes native libraries completely out of the equation. And to address @tonistiigi's concern about compile-time safety, third parties can be stopped from building it dynamically-linked by adding a `!cgo` build constraint to one or more critical files.
<details>
<summary>Proof of concept</summary>

```console
$ cat main.go
//go:build !cgo
// +build !cgo

package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os/user"
)

func main() {
	u, err := user.Lookup("docker")
	fmt.Println(u, err)
}
$ go build
package .: build constraints exclude all Go files in [path]
$ CGO_ENABLED=0 go build
$
```
</details>

With cgo out of the way, the most serious consequence of `archive/tar.TarInfoHeader` getting called while the process is chrooted would be a performance regression from repeatedly parsing `/etc/groups` for every file getting archived.

Of course, `docker-tar`, `docker-untar` and `docker-applyLayer` could all be compiled into a single binary so they all get the hardening benefits of static, cgo-less compilation while amortizing the disk usage across all three.
